Online Safety Filter for Deformable Object Manipulation
with Horizon Agnostic Neural Operators

Jiaxing Li    Hanjiang Hu    Zhuoyuan Wang Affiliation: All authors are with Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA. {jiaxingl, hanjianghu, zhuoyuaw, ynakahir, cliu6}@andrew.cmu.edu    Yorie Nakahira Affiliation: All authors are with Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA. {jiaxingl, hanjianghu, zhuoyuaw, ynakahir, cliu6}@andrew.cmu.edu    Changliu Liu ††thanks: *Equal contribution. Affiliation: All authors are with Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA. {jiaxingl, hanjianghu, zhuoyuaw, ynakahir, cliu6}@andrew.cmu.edu
Abstract

Safety-critical control of robotic manipulation tasks involving deformable media—such as fluids, cloth, and soft objects—remains challenging because existing learning-based approaches encode safety indirectly through reward shaping, which provides no guarantee of constraint satisfaction at deployment. We present a constraint-driven online safety filter for deformable-object manipulation that enforces explicit task-level safety constraints in real time by minimally modifying any nominal control policy. Our approach combines two key components: a horizon-agnostic neural operator that learns the boundary input-output mapping of the underlying PDE dynamics and generalizes across variable rollout lengths without retraining, and a boundary control barrier function that certifies safety at the task-relevant output level via a lightweight quadratic program. The resulting safety constraint is affine in the boundary-input rate, enabling real-time online filtering. We evaluate the proposed method on fluid manipulation tasks in FluidLab, where the filter improves safe-trajectory rates by up to 22% over unfiltered base policies while also reducing the number of steps required to reach the safe set, demonstrating that constraint-driven safety enforcement is both more reliable and more efficient than reward-shaping approaches.

I Introduction

Robots are increasingly deployed in manipulation tasks involving highly deformable media such as fluids, cloth, and soft objects. In these settings, safety is not merely about stability but about satisfying task-level constraints—avoiding spill, maintaining contact conditions, or keeping objects within designated regions—throughout execution. Most existing learning-based approaches for deformable manipulation are reward-driven [1, 2, 3, 4]: policies are trained to maximize task performance with safety encoded indirectly through penalties or data filtering. However, reward shaping does not guarantee constraint satisfaction, and policies often exhibit unsafe transient behaviors under disturbances or distribution shifts. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced when the underlying dynamics are governed by complex distributed phenomena, such as fluid–rigid interaction [5], where small control deviations can induce large state changes. These challenges call for a constraint-driven safety mechanism that operates online, enforces explicit task-level safety sets, and remains compatible with learned policies.

Achieving such constraint-driven safety for deformable manipulation requires two ingredients: a dynamics model that can predict task-relevant outcomes in real time, and a safety filter that can translate those predictions into hard constraints on the robot’s control actions. For manipulation tasks involving fluids or other deformable media, the underlying dynamics are governed by partial differential equations (PDEs), where the robot’s action enters as a boundary input and safety-relevant signals (e.g., object position, separation distance) are low-dimensional outputs of the temporal-spatial plant [6, 7]. Neural operators [8, 9, 10] can act as function-space approximators that learn input-to-output mappings of PDE systems, offering a promising route to fast, generalizable surrogate models for such dynamics [11]. In parallel, control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a principled, modular approach to safety filtering: they minimally modify a nominal control signal to enforce forward invariance of a user-defined safe set, typically via a lightweight quadratic program (QP) [12, 13]. However, combining neural-operator dynamics models with CBF-based safety filters for real-time, online use in robotic manipulation remains an open challenge.

In this paper, we address this challenge by developing an online constraint-driven safety filter for deformable-object manipulation, built around a horizon-agnostic neural operator and a boundary control barrier function (BCBF). The key insight is that, by training the neural operator on variable-length input prefixes, a single model can support safety filtering across arbitrary rollout lengths without retraining, enabling fully online deployment. The BCBF then operates at the boundary-output level, providing real-time safety certification that is compatible with any nominal policy while imposing only a minimal modification to the control signal. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We develop an online QP safety filter that pairs a time-dependent BCBF with a differentiable neural-operator surrogate. The resulting safety constraint is affine in the boundary input rate, making it solvable in real time.

  • •

    We introduce a horizon-agnostic training scheme for neural operators, enabling the same model to support online filtering at any rollout length without retraining.

  • •

    We evaluate the proposed method on complex fluid manipulation tasks, demonstrating that the online constraint-driven filter consistently outperforms both unfiltered base policies and an offline filter baseline by up to 22% while reducing the number of steps needed to reach the safe set.

II Related Work

II-A Deformable Object Manipulation in Robotics

Robotic manipulation of deformable objects—including cloth, fluids, and soft bodies—has attracted significant attention due to its relevance in household assistance, manufacturing, and laboratory automation. Compared to rigid-body manipulation, deformable systems exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear, and often partially observed dynamics, making modeling and control substantially more challenging [2, 3]. Textile manipulation has been extensively studied, emphasizing variability in material properties, perception under occlusion, and long-horizon planning [1, 2]. Recent benchmarks such as SoftGym [4] and FluidLab [5] enable reproducible evaluation of learning-based policies for cloth folding, fluid transport, and object gathering tasks. Complementary toolkits for soft and continuum robots, including SoMoGym [14] and SofaGym [15], further broaden the spectrum of deformable systems and control interfaces.

Most existing approaches rely on imitation learning or reinforcement learning to optimize task performance through reward maximization [1, 2, 3, 4]. While these methods have demonstrated promising results, safety is typically encoded indirectly via reward shaping, penalty terms, or data filtering. As a result, policies may exhibit unsafe transient behaviors, especially under long-horizon execution, disturbances, or distribution shift. This limitation is particularly acute in fluid manipulation, where small control deviations can induce large, irreversible state changes [5]. Explicit enforcement of task-level safety constraints during online execution remains underexplored in deformable manipulation settings.

Research Gap: Prior work in deformable manipulation focuses primarily on reward-driven policy optimization rather than constraint-driven safety enforcement, motivating the need for online safety mechanisms compatible with learned controllers.

II-B Neural Operators for Modeling PDE-Governed Dynamics

Many deformable manipulation tasks are naturally governed by distributed dynamics that can be modeled by partial differential equations (PDEs), such as fluid–rigid interaction and continuum deformation [7, 6]. Neural operators, including DeepONet [8] and Fourier neural operator (FNO) [10], have emerged as powerful tools for learning mappings between function spaces and approximating PDE solution operators [9]. These models generalize across discretizations and domain configurations, making them attractive for high-dimensional physical systems. More advanced neural operator architectures include graph-based neural operators [16], spectral neural operators [17], and physics-informed variants that combine data fitting with PDE constraints to achieve parametric PDE learning [18].

Recent work has explored neural operators for accelerating simulation, model-based control synthesis, and data-driven PDE prediction, including bypassing computationally heavy gain calculations in PDE backstepping [19, 20]. However, most applications focus on forward modeling or policy training rather than embedding neural operator models within real-time safety enforcement frameworks. In particular, their integration with constraint-based filtering mechanisms for robotics tasks remains limited.

Research Gap: While neural operators provide scalable surrogates for distributed dynamics, their use in online safety filtering for robotics manipulation tasks has not been systematically studied.

II-C Model-Based Safety Filters for Robotics

Model-based safety filters provide a principled mechanism for enforcing state or output constraints by minimally modifying nominal control inputs at runtime. Control barrier functions (CBFs) [12, 13] have been widely applied to robotic systems to guarantee forward invariance of safe sets, typically by solving a quadratic program at each control step to project nominal actions onto a constraint-satisfying region. Extensions of CBF address high relative-degree constraints [21, 22], sampled-data and delay effects [23], as well as robust and adaptive settings [24]. Reachability-based filters and safety-constrained model predictive control offer complementary perspectives and are surveyed alongside CBF-based methods in [25, 26]. Recent work further explores constructing robust safety filters online in challenging settings [27].

Most existing safety filters are developed for finite-dimensional dynamical systems and assume explicit state-space models. Extensions to infinite-dimensional or partially observed systems are more limited, and few works address safety enforcement when dynamics are governed by distributed PDE models [7, 6]. Recent safe PDE boundary control work proposes neural boundary control barrier functions (BCBFs) combined with differentiable neural operators to derive QP-based safety filtering for boundary outputs [11], providing the theoretical foundation our method builds upon. However, this prior work operates offline with fixed rollout lengths, limiting its applicability to robotics settings that require online, horizon-agnostic deployment.

Research Gap: Existing safety filters largely assume finite-dimensional models and do not address online constraint enforcement for PDE-governed deformable manipulation systems.

III Methodology

III-A Problem Formulation

We consider a general safety-critical control problem for systems governed by unknown partial differential equations (PDEs), where control is applied through boundary actuation and safety is specified on task-relevant outputs over a finite horizon. As a representative instance of this class, we focus on robotic manipulation with deformable media (e.g., fluid–rigid interaction). In this setting, we denote the overall coupled state as z⁡(x,t):𝒳×𝒯→𝒮z(x,t):\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}, where x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} is the spatial coordinate, t∈𝒯:=[0,T]t\in\mathcal{T}:=[0,T] is time, and 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space of the coupled robot–environment system.

Similar modeling paradigm is widely adopted in robotics for deformable object manipulation and soft robotic systems, where continuum theories (e.g., elasticity, Cosserat rod models, or fluid dynamics) [28] provide PDE descriptions of deformation and interaction with robots. Following the settings in [6], we model the deformable dynamics as

∂tz⁡(x,t)=𝒟⁡(z⁡(x,t),∇z​(x,t),∇2z​(x,t)),\partial_{t}z(x,t)=\mathcal{D}\!\left(z(x,t),\nabla z(x,t),\nabla^{2}z(x,t)\right), (1)

where 𝒟⁡(⋅)\mathcal{D}(\cdot) denotes unknown closed-loop PDE dynamics. The system is actuated through a Dirichlet boundary condition,

z⁡(0,t)=U⁡(t),z(0,t)=U(t), (2)

with a fixed initial condition z​(x,0)=z0​(x)z(x,0)=z_{0}(x), where U⁡(t)U(t) is the control input of the robot agent that is applied to the dynamics of the PDE.

We define the task-relevant boundary output as

Y⁡(t):=z⁡(xb,t),Y(t):=z(x_{b},t), (3)

where xb∈𝒳x_{b}\in\mathcal{X} denotes a designated boundary or observation location of interest. The output Y⁡(t)Y(t) may represent, as Figure 2 shows, the position of a transported object on XY plane, or a deformation magnitude, or a distance metric derived from the deformable state.

Classical state-dependent control barrier functions (CBFs) are difficult to apply directly in our setting. In PDE-governed robotic manipulation, safety is imposed on a low-dimensional task output Y⁡(t)Y(t), while the underlying state z⁡(x,t)z(x,t) is infinite-dimensional and only partially observed.

To bridge this mismatch, we adopt the boundary control barrier function (BCBF) framework from prior work [11], which certifies safety directly at the output boundary level. Let 𝒮0⊂𝒮\mathcal{S}_{0}\subset\mathcal{S} denote the user-defined safe set for the task output. Boundary-output safety over 𝒯=[0,T]\mathcal{T}=[0,T] is characterized by a finite-time feasibility condition: there exists t0∈𝒯t_{0}\in\mathcal{T} such that

∀t∈[t0,T],Y⁡(t)∈𝒮0.\forall\,t\in[t_{0},T],\quad Y(t)\in\mathcal{S}_{0}. (4)

This formulation serves as the theoretical safety foundation of our method. However, existing usage remains offline because direct neural operator-based BCBF construction typically assumes access to full trajectories, which is incompatible with real-time robotics execution.

III-B Horizon Agnostic Neural Operator

We model the boundary input-output mapping using a neural operator ℱθ:U⁡(t)→Y⁡(t)\mathcal{F}_{\theta}:U(t)\rightarrow Y(t) parameterized by θ\theta, which learns the transfer function from the boundary control input trajectory U⁡(t)U(t) to the boundary output trajectory Y⁡(t)Y(t). Following the construction in [9], the neural operator used is defined as

ℱθ=𝒬∘ℐL−1∘⋯∘ℐ0∘𝒫,\mathcal{F}_{\theta}=\mathcal{Q}\circ\mathcal{I}_{L-1}\circ\cdots\circ\mathcal{I}_{0}\circ\mathcal{P}, (5)

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} are pointwise lifting and projection operators (e.g., Fourier and inverse Fourier transforms in FNO [10]), and each ℐℓ\mathcal{I}_{\ell} is an integral kernel operator. Specifically, the ℓ\ell-th kernel integration layer is defined as

vℓ+1​(t)\displaystyle v_{\ell+1}(t) =ℐℓ​(vℓ)​(t)\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}_{\ell}(v_{\ell})(t) (6)
=σℓ+1​(Wℓ​vℓ​(t)+∫𝒯κ(ℓ)​(t,s)​vℓ​(s)​ds+bℓ​(t)),\displaystyle=\sigma_{\ell+1}\Big(W_{\ell}v_{\ell}(t)+\int_{\mathcal{T}}\kappa^{(\ell)}(t,s)\,v_{\ell}(s)\,ds+b_{\ell}(t)\Big),

for ℓ=0,…,L−1\ell=0,\dots,L-1, where vℓ:𝒯→ℝdℓv_{\ell}:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}} denotes the hidden representation at layer ℓ\ell, σℓ+1​(⋅)\sigma_{\ell+1}(\cdot) is a nonlinear activation function, Wℓ∈ℝdℓ+1×dℓW_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell+1}\times d_{\ell}} is a local linear operator, κ(ℓ)∈C⁡(𝒯×𝒯,ℝdℓ+1×dℓ)\kappa^{(\ell)}\in C(\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T};\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell+1}\times d_{\ell}}) is a learnable kernel function, and bℓ​(t)b_{\ell}(t) is a bias term.

To enable real-time safety filtering in robotics without committing to a fixed rollout length, we train a single horizon-agnostic neural operator that is valid over variable-horizon prefixes. This design allows deployment under receding-horizon execution and avoids retraining when task duration changes. Let 𝒟={(Uk,Yk)}k=1K\mathcal{D}=\{(U_{k},Y_{k})\}_{k=1}^{K} be trajectory pairs sampled from the unknown closed-loop PDE dynamics and discretized at {tm}m=1M\{t_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}, where Uk={Uk​(tm)}m=1MU_{k}=\{U_{k}(t_{m})\}_{m=1}^{M} and Yk={Yk​(tm)}m=1MY_{k}=\{Y_{k}(t_{m})\}_{m=1}^{M}. During training, we sample a prefix length M~∈[Mmin,Mmax]\tilde{M}\in[M_{\min},M_{\max}] and feed Uk1:M~U_{k}^{1:\tilde{M}} into ℱθ\mathcal{F}_{\theta}, which induces the horizon-agnostic empirical risk.

ℒ\displaystyle\mathcal{L} =𝔼M~∼𝒰⁡[Mmin,Mmax][1K∑k=1K1M~∑m=1M~\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{M}\sim\mathcal{U}[M_{\min},M_{\max}]}\Bigg[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{\tilde{M}}\sum_{m=1}^{\tilde{M}} (7)
‖Yk(tm)−ℱθ(Uk1:M~)(tm)‖22].\displaystyle\left\|Y_{k}(t_{m})-\mathcal{F}_{\theta}\!\left(U_{k}^{1:\tilde{M}}\right)(t_{m})\right\|_{2}^{2}\Bigg].

Hence, the same ℱθ\mathcal{F}_{\theta} is optimized over a distribution of prefix lengths and queried online with ascending-length control histories. In practice, this turns horizon-agnostic learning into a deployment capability for prefix-based real-time safety certification without fixed-horizon assumptions.

III-C Online Filtering

We implement online filtering in a receding one-step manner at each discrete time ti=i​Δ​tt_{i}=i\Delta t. Let uiu_{i} denote the nominal boundary control from the base policy, and let u^i\hat{u}_{i} denote the filtered control applied to the system. At step ii, the filter keeps the previously applied filtered sequence and appends the current nominal control uiu_{i}, and forms the prefix input

U~0:i:={u^0,…,u^i−1,ui}.\tilde{U}_{0:i}:=\{\hat{u}_{0},\ldots,\hat{u}_{i-1},u_{i}\}. (8)

The neural operator then predicts the boundary-output prefix Y^0:i=ℱθ(U~0:i)\hat{Y}_{0:i}=\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(\tilde{U}_{0:i}),

Using the current observation yiy_{i}, we evaluate the BCBF terms ϕi:=ϕ⁡(yi,ti)\phi_{i}:=\phi(y_{i},t_{i}) and solve the following one-step quadratic programming (QP) for the safe control gradient U˙safe​(ti)\dot{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}(t_{i}):

U˙safe​(ti)\displaystyle\dot{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}(t_{i}) =arg⁡minU˙​‖U˙−U˙nominal​(ti)‖,\displaystyle=\arg\min_{\dot{U}}\big\|\,\dot{U}-\dot{U}_{\mathrm{nominal}}(t_{i})\,\big\|, (9)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} ϕ˙​(yi,ti)+α​ϕ​(yi,ti)+C​ϕ0≤0,\displaystyle\dot{\phi}(y_{i},t_{i})+\alpha\phi(y_{i},t_{i})+C\phi_{0}\leq 0,

where ϕ0=ϕ⁡(0,Y0)\phi_{0}=\phi(0,Y_{0}) and ϕ˙\dot{\phi} is composed by

ϕ˙=∂yϕ⋅Y˙+∂tϕ.\dot{\phi}={\partial}_{y}\phi\cdot\dot{Y}+\partial_{t}\phi. (10)

Here, Y˙\dot{Y} can be obtained from the trained neural operator with the linear dependence on U˙​(t)\dot{U}(t), which has been proven by [11].

Given that the BCBF constraint (9) is linear with respect to U˙\dot{U}, it can thus be framed and solved by a QP solver. Given the solved U˙safe​(ti)\dot{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}(t_{i}), we address the potential model mismatch between the trained neural operator ℱθ\mathcal{F}_{\theta} and real underlying PDE dynamics with a filtering threshold β\beta such that

U˙​(ti)={U˙safe​(ti),‖U˙safe​(ti)−U˙nominal​(ti)‖≤β,U˙nominal​(ti),otherwise.\dot{U}(t_{i})=\begin{cases}\dot{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}(t_{i}),&\|\dot{U}_{\mathrm{safe}}(t_{i})-\dot{U}_{\mathrm{nominal}}(t_{i})\|\leq\beta,\\ \dot{U}_{\mathrm{nominal}}(t_{i}),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (11)

with the final control signal at the time step tit_{i} is calculated by ui=ui−1+Δ​t⋅U˙​(ti)u_{i}=u_{i-1}+\Delta t\cdot\dot{U}(t_{i}).

The online filtering procedures are summarized in Algorithm 1.

IV Experimental Results

IV-A Experimental Setup

We evaluate the proposed method in FluidLab [5], a differentiable fluid-rigid interaction simulator. FluidLab is a testbed for safe boundary control of PDE-governed robotic manipulation, where coupled high-dimensional deformable dynamics can be simulated. With this testbed, we learn the input-output operator U↦YU\mapsto Y and train BCBFs from data, and evaluate online filtering under matched nominal/filtered conditions. In all experiments, we use 200200 control steps for data collection rollouts and execute real-time control at a frequency of 500500Hz. Trajectory-level and step-level safety metrics are used for analysis.

IV-A1 Transporting Task

The transporting environment contains a rigid cube interacting with surrounding fluid in a planar boundary-locked workspace. The robot agent ejects water with constant speed and is required to transport the target cube into the specified region, and through which the policy is able to control the robot’s linear speed on the xx axis and the angular speed, which we denote by U⁡(t)∈ℝ2U(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. The task-relevant boundary state Y⁡(t)Y(t) is constructed from cube planar coordinates and used by the learned model and BCBF. The safe set is defined as a geometric target region in the xx-yy plane:

𝒮0trans={Y:x∈[0.05,0.25],y∈[0.65,0.95]}.\mathcal{S}_{0}^{\mathrm{trans}}=\{Y:x\in[0.05,0.25],\;y\in[0.65,0.95]\}.

A rollout is safe at a step if the cube center lies in 𝒮0trans\mathcal{S}_{0}^{\mathrm{trans}}; distance to this set is additionally recorded as a continuous safety margin.

IV-A2 Gathering Task

The gathering environment contains two rigid bodies immersed in fluid, and the robot equipped with a rigid spatula that is able to paddle the water and specified to reduce the rigid bodies’ separation. The policy outputs boundary control signal U⁡(t)∈ℝ2U(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} which commands its linear speed on X,YX,Y plane. The boundary state Y⁡(t)Y(t) is defined from object-relative quantities (difference of object positions) and, in the scalar setting, by an auxiliary safety variable s⁡(t)s(t) that is the distance between the two bodies. The safe set is defined by a distance threshold:

𝒮0gather={Y:‖p1−p2‖2<δ},δ=0.2.\mathcal{S}_{0}^{\mathrm{gather}}=\{Y:\|p_{1}-p_{2}\|_{2}<\delta\},\quad\delta=0.2.

IV-B Implementation Details

Base policy and data generation. The base policy is a noisy proportional controller with task-specific geometric priors. Let clip[ℓ,u]​(⋅)\mathrm{clip}_{[\ell,u]}(\cdot) denote component-wise clipping to [ℓ,u][\ell,u], and let ηi∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)\eta_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) denote injected control noise.

For transporting, define robot planar position pir=[xir,yir]⊤p_{i}^{r}=[x_{i}^{r},y_{i}^{r}]^{\top}, yaw ψi\psi_{i}, and target point pic=[xic,yic]⊤p_{i}^{c}=[x_{i}^{c},y_{i}^{c}]^{\top} (cube-related reference from the simulator state). The two effective control channels are forward velocity and yaw rate, Ui=[vi,ωi]⊤U_{i}=[v_{i},\omega_{i}]^{\top}. The translational component is

vi={clip[−vmax,vmax]​(kp​(xic−xir)+ηx,i),xir<xic,clip[−vmax,vmax]​(kp​(xic−xir)+ηx,i),xir>xic+d,0,otherwise,v_{i}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{clip}_{[-v_{\max},v_{\max}]}\!\left(k_{p}(x_{i}^{c}-x_{i}^{r})+\eta_{x,i}\right),&x_{i}^{r}<x_{i}^{c},\\[5.69054pt] \mathrm{clip}_{[-v_{\max},v_{\max}]}\!\left(k_{p}(x_{i}^{c}-x_{i}^{r})+\eta_{x,i}\right),&x_{i}^{r}>x_{i}^{c}+d,\\[5.69054pt] 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (12)

where d>0d>0 is the distance margin that keeps the robot behind the cube before pushing and kpk_{p} is the gain. The yaw channel aligns the robot heading to the target:

ψi⋆=atan2⁡(yic−yir,xic−xir),eψ,i=mod⁡(θ+π,2​π)−π,\psi_{i}^{\star}=\operatorname{atan2}(y_{i}^{c}-y_{i}^{r},\;x_{i}^{c}-x_{i}^{r}),\qquad e_{\psi,i}=\operatorname{mod}(\theta+\pi,2\pi)-\pi, (13)
ωi={clip[−ωmax,ωmax]​(kω​eψ,i+ηω,i),|eψ,i|>εψ,0,otherwise.\omega_{i}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{clip}_{[-\omega_{\max},\omega_{\max}]}\!\left(k_{\omega}e_{\psi,i}+\eta_{\omega,i}\right),&|e_{\psi,i}|>\varepsilon_{\psi},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (14)

where eψ,ie_{\psi,i} is the mismatch between robot’s heading and the actual robot-to-target angle. In our implementation, vmax=ωmax=1v_{\max}=\omega_{\max}=1, d=0.15d=0.15, and εψ=0.05\varepsilon_{\psi}=0.05.

For gathering, the robot tracks an elliptical reference trajectory in the horizontal plane. Let (xc,yc)(x_{c},y_{c}) be the ellipse center, a,ba,b the semi-axes, ϑ\vartheta the ellipse orientation, and ρ\rho the speed-scale factor. With θi∈[0,2​π​ρ]\theta_{i}\in[0,2\pi\rho], the reference is

[xirefyiref]=[xcyc]+[cos⁡ϑ−sin⁡ϑsin⁡ϑcos⁡ϑ]​[acosθibsinθi].\begin{bmatrix}x_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}\\ y_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{c}\\ y_{c}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\cos\vartheta&-\sin\vartheta\\ \sin\vartheta&\cos\vartheta\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\cos\theta_{i}\\ b\sin\theta_{i}\end{bmatrix}. (15)

The effective boundary control Ui=[vx,i,vy,i]⊤U_{i}=[v_{x,i},v_{y,i}]^{\top} is

vx,i\displaystyle v_{x,i} =clip[umin,umax]​(kp​(xiref−xir)+ηx,i),\displaystyle=\mathrm{clip}_{[u_{\min},u_{\max}]}\!\left(k_{p}(x_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}-x_{i}^{r})+\eta_{x,i}\right), (16)
vy,i\displaystyle v_{y,i} =clip[umin,umax]​(kp​(yiref−yir)+ηy,i).\displaystyle=\mathrm{clip}_{[u_{\min},u_{\max}]}\!\left(k_{p}(y_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}-y_{i}^{r})+\eta_{y,i}\right).

Horizon-agnostic neural operator training. The NO training pipeline uses preprocessed task trajectories and selects ntrainn_{\mathrm{train}} and ntestn_{\mathrm{test}} episodes for training and testing, respectively. Each episode has horizon M=200M=200 before optional temporal subsampling. Let one batch contain episodes {(Ub,Yb)}b=1B\{(U_{b},Y_{b})\}_{b=1}^{B}, where Ub∈ℝM×2U_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times 2} and Yb∈ℝM×dyY_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d_{y}} (task-dependent dyd_{y}). The collate function samples one prefix length per batch

M~\displaystyle\tilde{M} ∼𝒰⁡{Mmin,…,Mmax},\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{U}\{M_{\min},\ldots,M_{\max}\}, (17)

and crops all trajectories to the first M~\tilde{M} steps

U~b=Ub[:M~],Y~b=Yb[:M~].\tilde{U}_{b}=U_{b}[1\!:\!\tilde{M}],\qquad\tilde{Y}_{b}=Y_{b}[1\!:\!\tilde{M}].

Hence, all samples in one batch share the same length, while M~\tilde{M} changes across batches, which directly realizes horizon-agnostic training. The Fourier neural operator used has 6464 hidden channels, 44 layers and the frequency latent embeddings is truncated to keep the lowest 1616 frequency modes. The model is trained using the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 1​e−31\mathrm{e}{-}3 and a weight decay of 1​e−31\mathrm{e}{-}3.

BCBF network and optimization. The BCBF model is an MLP ϕψ:ℝ1+dy→ℝ\phi_{\psi}:\mathbb{R}^{1+d_{y}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} with hidden widths [32,128,64,32][32,128,64,32], where the input is [t,Y][t,Y]. Training data are the same task rollouts sampled by ntrainn_{\mathrm{train}}, ntestn_{\mathrm{test}}, reshaped over all time points in each trajectory. For each batch, we construct

𝐲t​t=[t,Y],𝐔0=[t0,Y0],𝐘˙=[1,d​Yd​t],\mathbf{y}_{tt}=[t,Y],\quad\mathbf{U}_{0}=[t_{0},Y_{0}],\quad\dot{\mathbf{Y}}=\left[1,\frac{dY}{dt}\right],

where d​Y/d​tdY/dt is computed through finite difference. We followed the BCBF loss formulation in [11], with NAdam optimizer with betas 0.9,0.9990.9,0.999, weight decay 0.10.1, and learning rate 0.010.01.

IV-C Results

Table I shows safety and convergence comparison between nominal and filtered policies, where online filtering consistently improves safety in both tasks at the trajectory level. In transporting, the filtered policy increases the safe-trajectory rate from 57.8%57.8\% to 80.2%80.2\%, which is a gain of 22.4%22.4\% over the base policy. Figure 3 shows the base and filtered target trajectories, where the base policy results in stagnation and the filtered policy successfully transported to the set of targets. In gathering, the safe-trajectory rate increases from 45.5%45.5\% to 63.6%63.6\%, which is an improvement of 18.1%18.1\%. These gains indicate that the filter improves the probability that an entire rollout remains or becomes safe under the same base policy backbone. Figure 4 visualizes the control inputs, distance evolution, and the trajectories of the two target objects in the XY plane. The base policy fails to converge to the required target distance and, at a later stage, pushes the objects farther apart. This behavior is confirmed by the distance evolution plot in Figure 4, where the distance increases around t≈0.25t\approx 0.25s. To better understand this phenomenon, we examine simulation snapshots sampled at 0.1s intervals. Around t=0.3t=0.3s, the base policy generates noticeable turbulence while maneuvering the spatula back toward the paddle position. This disturbance induces additional water flow that pushes the objects away from each other, preventing convergence. In contrast, the filtered policy avoids this behavior by adaptively steering the spatula to mitigate water disturbance, thereby maintaining stable convergence toward the desired distance.

At the step level, the filtered policy also reduces the average number of steps required to reach convergence to the safe condition. In transporting, this metric drops from 179.18179.18 to 169.54169.54 (9.649.64 fewer steps, ≈5.4%\approx 5.4\% reduction). In gathering, it decreases from 166.81166.81 to 160.36160.36 (6.456.45 fewer steps, ≈3.9%\approx 3.9\% reduction). Since trajectories that reach the safe set earlier spend fewer timesteps in unsafe transients, this reduction provides evidence of improved cumulative step-level safety behavior in addition to higher trajectory-level safety rates.

Moreover, for both transporting and gathering, we observe that applying a neural operator trained offline as a fixed filter degrades performance, as shown in Table I. The safety rate decreases, and convergence requires more steps than the base policy. This result highlights that the safety filter must be adapted online to the current base policy and environment dynamics in order to provide consistent improvement.

Taken together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed online filter, across different safety geometries including region-reaching safety (transporting) and pairwise-distance safety (gathering). The proposed method improves rollout-level safety success rates while simultaneously reducing cumulative unsafe exposure over time.

V Conclusion

This paper presents an online safety filtering framework for manipulating deformable objects whose dynamics is governed by a PDE system. We combine a horizon-agnostic neural operator for variable-horizon boundary input-output modeling with a BCBF-based quadratic-program safety filter that runs at each control cycle. The resulting pipeline preserves the nominal policy structure while enforcing task-level safety constraints through minimal control modification. Experiments on FluidLab transporting and gathering tasks show improved safe-trajectory rates and reduced steps to safety convergence compared with the nominal policy. Future work will study transfer to broader deformable manipulation domains and hardware-in-the-loop deployment with tighter real-time guarantees.
